name: Subclinical (mild autonomous cortisol secretion) Cushing syndrome

reference.source: Williams Textbook of Endocrinology / ESE-ENSAT Clinical Practice Guideline on the Management of Adrenal Incidentalomas
clinicalPearls: Refers to autonomous cortisol secretion from an adrenal adenoma without the overt clinical features of Cushing syndrome; current guidance favours the term mild autonomous cortisol secretion (MACS)
It is typically identified during evaluation of an adrenal incidentaloma
The diagnosis is biochemical, resting principally on failure to suppress cortisol after an overnight low-dose dexamethasone suppression test, with a suppressed or low ACTH supporting adrenal autonomy
Although termed subclinical, it is associated with increased cardiometabolic morbidity, including hypertension, type 2 diabetes, dyslipidaemia, central obesity and reduced bone density
Post-dexamethasone cortisol thresholds stratify risk, with higher values indicating more definite autonomous secretion
Management is individualised: treat the associated comorbidities and consider adrenalectomy in younger patients with significant secretion and attributable disease
Perioperative and post-adrenalectomy glucocorticoid cover is needed because the contralateral adrenal gland may be suppressed
reference.pathophysiology: An adrenocortical adenoma secretes cortisol semi-autonomously, partly escaping normal hypothalamic-pituitary feedback. The circulating cortisol, although insufficient to produce classic Cushingoid features, suppresses pituitary ACTH and the contralateral adrenal cortex. Chronic mild cortisol excess drives insulin resistance, hypertension, visceral adiposity and bone loss, which explains the cardiometabolic and skeletal consequences despite the absence of florid clinical signs.
additionalDifferentials: Pseudo-Cushing states related to alcohol, depression or obesity
Phaeochromocytoma as part of the incidentaloma workup
additionalInvestigations: Overnight low-dose dexamethasone suppression test as the key screening test
Plasma ACTH, expected to be low or suppressed, and DHEAS
Late-night salivary cortisol and 24-hour urinary free cortisol to gauge overall cortisol burden
Assessment of comorbidities including blood pressure, glucose or HbA1c, lipids and bone density
Adrenal CT to characterise the adenoma
Metanephrines and aldosterone-to-renin ratio as part of the incidentaloma screen
redFlags: Marked post-dexamethasone cortisol elevation together with significant comorbidity
Imaging features suggesting malignancy in the adrenal lesion
Unrecognised adrenal insufficiency after adrenalectomy from contralateral suppression
reference.prognosis: Often stable, but untreated mild autonomous cortisol secretion carries excess cardiometabolic and fracture risk and higher mortality than a non-functioning adenoma; selected patients improve after adrenalectomy.
pitfalls: Dismissing subclinical secretion as clinically irrelevant and neglecting cardiometabolic risk
Relying on a single test without confirming autonomy and excluding pseudo-Cushing states
Forgetting perioperative and postoperative steroid cover after adrenalectomy
Missing contralateral adrenal suppression and precipitating an adrenal crisis
references: ESE-ENSAT Clinical Practice Guideline on the Management of Adrenal Incidentalomas
management: Confirm autonomous cortisol secretion biochemically with the overnight low-dose dexamethasone suppression test and characterise the adenoma before deciding management
Treat associated cardiometabolic comorbidities: hypertension, type 2 diabetes or glucose intolerance, dyslipidaemia and central obesity
Assess bone density and treat osteoporosis to reduce fracture risk
Adrenalectomy considered in younger patients with more definite autonomous secretion and attributable comorbidity
Perioperative glucocorticoid cover and postoperative steroid replacement for the suppressed contralateral adrenal after adrenalectomy
Surveillance of patients managed non-operatively, monitoring cortisol secretion, adenoma size and evolving comorbidities
